note: Fables attributed to Aesop became one of the principal ancient reference corpora for the brief exemplary tale: fictive situations, often involving animals, used to illustrate a point or support an argument. The corpus itself remained fluid across oral and written transmission.
source_label: Oxford Classical Dictionary — Aesop

note: The Grimms gathered tales from oral and mixed oral-literary networks in order to preserve traditions they believed were disappearing; later editions increasingly reshaped the material for literary readers.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — How the Grimm Brothers Saved the Fairy Tale

note: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected, edited, published, and repeatedly revised Children and Household Tales across multiple editions beginning in 1812.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities

note: The Grimms' collection became one of the most influential printed vehicles through which European fairy-tale forms and motifs circulated internationally, especially in children's culture.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities

note: Jack London wrote The Call of the Wild.
source_label: Travel Yukon — The story of Jack London

note: London traveled to the Yukon during the 1897 Klondike Gold Rush. He did not become rich from mining, but the journey supplied direct experience of northern landscape, travel, hardship, people, and stories that became literary material.
source_label: Travel Yukon — The story of Jack London

note: Yukon authorities explicitly connect London's Klondike experiences to The Call of the Wild and White Fang; the novel's northern world is rooted in material he encountered during the gold-rush journey.
source_label: Travel Yukon — The story of Jack London

note: Franz Kafka wrote The Metamorphosis in 1912; it was first published in 1915.
source_label: Franz Kafka Museum — Timeline

note: Kafka worked for the Workers' Accident Insurance Institute from 1908 to 1922. The job placed him inside a large administrative system dealing with industrial labor and accident claims while he maintained what the museum describes as a difficult 'double life' between office work and writing.
source_label: Franz Kafka Museum — Employment

note: Kafka belonged to the informal Prague Circle of German-writing authors and developed important friendships with figures including Max Brod; this sits within his multilingual Prague and Jewish cultural environment.
source_label: Franz Kafka Museum — Timeline

note: Kurt Vonnegut wrote Slaughterhouse-Five, published in 1969 after decades of trying to find a form for his Dresden material.
source_label: National WWII Museum — Kurt Vonnegut and Slaughterhouse-Five

note: Vonnegut served in the U.S. Army, fought with the 106th Infantry Division, was captured during the Battle of the Bulge, and became a prisoner of war in Germany.
source_label: National WWII Museum

note: Vonnegut was a prisoner of war in Dresden during the February 1945 bombing, survived in an underground meat locker beneath the slaughterhouse where he was held, and later worked amid the destroyed city. The event remains a World node; his personal encounter with it is expressed by this edge.
source_label: National WWII Museum

note: The bombing of Dresden is the central historical event repeatedly represented and transformed in Slaughterhouse-Five. Vonnegut's firsthand experience is separately represented through Dresden → Vonnegut, avoiding the collapse of event history and biography into one node.
source_label: National WWII Museum

note: Mary O'Hare objected to framing the very young soldiers as glamorous movie-war heroes or making war look good. Vonnegut later said her criticism gave him an important clue to the book's approach, making this a documented person-to-work creative intervention rather than historical context.
source_label: The Paris Review — Kurt Vonnegut interview excerpt

note: Arthur Conan Doyle created Sherlock Holmes, beginning with A Study in Scarlet.
source_label: British Library — Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes

note: Conan Doyle studied under Joseph Bell at Edinburgh and observed Bell infer patients' occupations and backgrounds from minute physical details. Doyle later explicitly credited Bell with the observational model he amplified into Holmes.
source_label: PBS — Sir Arthur Conan Doyle

note: Conan Doyle wrote that he owed Sherlock Holmes to Bell and described building a scientific detective around the deduction, inference, and observation he had watched Bell practice.
source_label: Journal of Urology — Dr Joseph Bell and Sherlock Holmes

note: Conan Doyle explicitly praised Poe's Dupin stories as foundational detective fiction; Cambridge scholarship identifies Dupin as Holmes's literary model and notes Doyle's deliberate acknowledgement of him inside A Study in Scarlet.
source_label: Cambridge — The Case of Sherlock Holmes

note: Conan Doyle called Poe the supreme original short-story writer and traced modern detective fiction back to Dupin, making Poe a directly acknowledged literary predecessor rather than a retrospective genre comparison.
source_label: Cambridge — The Case of Sherlock Holmes

note: C. S. Lewis wrote The Chronicles of Narnia.
source_label: C. S. Lewis Foundation — Reading The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe with Lewis

note: Lewis said the Narnian books began as pictures in his head, especially a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels in a snowy wood; later a lion entered the developing story and pulled the narrative together.
source_label: C. S. Lewis Foundation — Lewis on Narnia's origin

note: Lewis explicitly said that as the originating images became a story they seemed to demand the fairy-tale form, whose brevity and traditional flexibility he embraced.
source_label: C. S. Lewis — Sometimes Fairy Stories May Say Best What's to Be Said

note: Neil Gaiman created the modern Sandman series for DC beginning in 1989.
source_label: The Guardian — How we made The Sandman

note: Gaiman says Roger Zelazny's Lord of Light showed him a way to make gods function with something like superhero energy; he describes thinking that although he could not do superheroes, he could do 'god comics.'
source_label: The Guardian — Neil Gaiman on The Sandman

note: Neil Gaiman wrote American Gods.
source_label: The Guardian — Neil Gaiman on writing American Gods

note: Gaiman says American Gods cohered during a 1998 Reykjavik stopover when a Leif Erikson display made him wonder whether migrants brought their gods with them to America.
source_label: The Guardian — Neil Gaiman on writing American Gods

evidence: explicit mythic reuse / author composition account
note: American Gods directly reuses Old Norse deities and migration traditions, including Odin, within its larger argument about gods traveling with believers; Gaiman's own account of the book's origin begins with Leif Erikson and imported gods.
source_label: The Guardian — Neil Gaiman on writing American Gods

note: Anne McCaffrey wrote the early Pern stories that were combined and expanded into Dragonflight.
source_label: The Worlds of Anne McCaffrey — FAQ

note: McCaffrey identified Austin Tappan Wright's Islandia as highly influential when she read it at about age fourteen.
source_label: Dragon Con interview with Anne McCaffrey

note: The first Pern material appeared in Analog. McCaffrey's own project history describes developing Pern from the question 'what if dragons were the good guys?'; the Analog editorial environment then helped expand the concept into dragons fighting Thread and a larger science-fictional system.
source_label: The Worlds of Anne McCaffrey — FAQ

note: Michael Lewis wrote The Big Short as narrative nonfiction about the subprime mortgage collapse and the people who recognized the system's failures.
source_label: PBS NewsHour — Michael Lewis on The Big Short

note: Lewis has described Tom Wolfe as his first enduring literary hero and as a central model for making researched nonfiction read with the force and character-focus of narrative.
source_label: The Guardian — Michael Lewis profile

note: The book investigates the subprime mortgage system and financial collapse by following people who saw deteriorating lending standards, ratings failures, and mispriced mortgage risk before the broader system did.
source_label: PBS NewsHour — Michael Lewis on The Big Short

note: Lewis says the characters were the 'oxygen' of the narrative: by following people in conflict with the system, he could make complex financial machinery understandable and give readers a reason to care about it.
source_label: PBS NewsHour — Michael Lewis on character-driven explanation

note: Agatha Christie wrote Murder on the Orient Express, first serialized in 1933 and published as a novel in 1934.
source_label: AgathaChristie.com — Facts about Murder on the Orient Express

note: Christie's estate identifies the Lindbergh kidnapping as a partial inspiration for the fictional Armstrong kidnapping case; she transformed real details rather than reproducing the case literally.
source_label: AgathaChristie.com — The case that inspired Murder on the Orient Express

note: A real 1929 incident left the Orient Express trapped by snow for days. Christie's estate identifies this, alongside her own train travel, as part of the real-world material behind the snowbound setting.
source_label: AgathaChristie.com — Facts about Murder on the Orient Express
